Rail & roads · Kenya

Road reserves, railway reserves and fibre routes in Kenya

Road and railway reserves carry more than traffic. Kiosks, stalls and workshops line them, fibre and pipes run inside them, and the first rails of the new standard gauge line from Naivasha to Kisumu and Malaba were laid in July 2026. We map what stands in each reserve and what has changed along each route between dated images, by segment, and a person checks each result.

Request a proposal Fibre routes

Road reserves

What stands on the road reserve, segment by segment

The Kenya Roads Act says nobody may “erect, construct or lay, or establish any structure or other thing, on or over or below the surface of a road reserve or land in a building restricted area” without the road authority’s written permission (section 49(1)). We map what stands there, by segment: kiosks, stalls, mabati structures, jua kali sheds, walls and houses inside the reserve, and, where you send it, inside the building restricted area beyond it.

Each structure the review confirms is listed with its distance from the centreline or the reserve edge, its chainage and its coordinates, and each 500 m segment is rated by the number of structures it holds. Repeat scans flag new and removed structures between dated images, confirmed by a reviewer, so the road authority’s teams can follow up through their own process, and so a widening or dualling design can be checked against what actually stands beside the road.

What you receive

  • A register of structures in the reserve and the building restricted area
  • Distances, chainage and coordinates for each
  • A rating for each 500 m segment
  • New and removed structures at each repeat scan
  • A PDF report in English and GIS layers

Rail and roads across Africa

Railway reserves and new lines

Before construction, during it, and after opening

The standard gauge extension runs about 264 km from Naivasha to Kisumu, with an 8.69 km spur to the new Kisumu port, and a further 107 km from Kisumu to Malaba. Phase 2B passes through Narok, Bomet, Nyamira, Kericho and Kisumu counties, and phase 2C through Kisumu, Siaya, Vihiga, Kakamega and Busia (KBC, 21 March 2026), and the first rails and sleepers were laid on 1 and 2 July 2026 (Kenya Railways, 3 July 2026). New lines like this need dated records at three moments.

Baseline

Before construction

A dated register of the structures along the alignment and in the reserve before the preliminary survey and the notices, to support the acquisition, the census and the compensation that follow.

Progress

During construction

Cleared ground, earthworks, camps and laydown areas along the alignment between scans, and, where drones fly, orthophotos and elevation models compared side by side with maps of cut and fill.

The reserve

After opening

Repeat scans of the railway reserve, flagging new structures and works between dated images so the reserve can be kept as the design left it.

The Kenya Railways Corporation Act text we read sets no reserve width, so the register uses the reserve you send us as a polygon, or the widths per section. We map structures, never people, and we do not decide which structures are authorised.

Fibre routes

New works along buried fibre, found between dated images

About 13,000 km of national backbone fibre is in place (Capital FM, 15 October 2025), the Digital Superhighway programme aims to “roll out 100,000 km of fibre optic cable nationwide” (Capital FM, 30 January 2026), and a government-funded project is extending fibre to more than 53,000 public institutions.

Much fibre runs in road reserves. Satellites can’t see a cut cable, but they can show new excavations, earthworks, tracks and structures along the route between dated images, so patrols go where the ground has changed. Each flag carries its location, its distance to the route and the dates of the images on either side of the change, and a reviewer confirms it before it reaches you.

Relocation on request

The Kenya Roads Act requires pipe-borne and wire-borne utilities in a road reserve, expressly including “fibre optic cable”, to be relocated “at no cost to the Authority” on the road authority’s written request, and removed within sixty days of notice; otherwise the authority removes them at the provider’s cost (section 27).

When a relocation notice arrives, we compare alternative routes for the cable by the structures and excavation each would cross, and record what stands along the new route before the work starts.

Excavation and ground-disturbance mapping

Wayleaves along the way

Counties, forests and other crossings

In August 2025 a government Principal Secretary cited the “high fees and levies demanded by county governments including wayleave acquisition challenges” as a hurdle for fibre builders (KBC, 15 August 2025), and routes that leave the road reserve need their own wayleaves across public, community and private land under the Land Act (sections 143–148). A route comparison that counts the structures, parcels of cleared land and forest cover each option crosses helps choose between staying in the reserve and leaving it.

We describe the ground. The permissions, the fees and the negotiations with counties and landowners stay with your wayleave team.

What these registers are not

  • Not a cadastral or boundary survey: those are for surveyors under the Survey Act
  • Not a record of who owns or occupies a structure
  • Not a decision on whether a structure is authorised
  • Not real-time: each flag compares two dated images

Frequently asked questions

How wide is the road reserve you measure?

The one that applies to your road. Reserve widths are not published in the sources we checked, and they differ by road and by section, so send the reserve and any building restricted area as polygons, or the widths either side of the centreline per section, and each structure is reported with its distance and its band.

Do you map kiosks and stalls in the road reserve?

Yes, as structures. Each one is listed with its location, its distance from the carriageway centreline or the reserve edge, and the date it first appears in the imagery. We do not identify traders or owners, and whether a structure has the road authority’s written permission under section 49 of the Kenya Roads Act is for the road authority to decide.

Can you see a cut or damaged fibre cable?

No. A buried cable is invisible from above. What imagery shows is new excavations, trenches, earthworks, tracks and structures along the route between two dated images, so patrols and repair crews go where the ground has changed.

Can you track construction on a new railway?

Yes, from the land side. Dated satellite imagery shows cleared ground, earthworks, camps, laydown areas and new structures along the alignment between scans. Where drone orthophotos and elevation models are flown, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, we compare them side by side and map where ground has been cut or filled.

Do you map riparian reserves?

Yes, at the width you give us. “Public land” in the Land Act includes reserves under the Survey Act (section 2), but riparian widths are not published in the sources we checked, so send the width or the reserve polygon along each watercourse and we list the structures inside it.

Send the road, rail or fibre route

A route file or reserve polygons, the counties, the reserve or restricted-area widths per section and what the register is for. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
